## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/03.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Design Innovation in Assessment
• In response to the pandemic, the Center pivoted to host the
RILS conference virtually in 2021.
• Spearheaded by Jeri Thompson (now retired) and myself, the
conference centered on the pivotal concept of &quot;Design
Innovation&quot; in educational assessment.
• The aim was to capitalize on the extensive momentum in
design innovation, exploring its applicability to modernizing
and enhancing assessment development.</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/04.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">First Exposure to Design Thinking
• My introduction to Design Thinking originated in the early
2010s through my involvement in software development for
the SchoolView data visualization platform.
• Concepts such as &quot;Agile Development,&quot; &quot;Scrums,&quot; &quot;Personas,&quot;
and &quot;Prototyping&quot; became integral to our development
dialogue.
• At that time, I began to ponder the potential for these design
methodologies to enhance the Center's work in educational
assessment and accountability system design.</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">A Brief Introduction to Design Thinking</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/07.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">What is Design Thinking?
• Definition: Design Thinking is a human-centered approach to problem-solving that
focuses on understanding user needs, ideation, prototyping, and iteration.
• Core Phases:
• Empathize
• Define
• Ideate
• Prototype
• Test
• Importance: Allows for creative solutions to complex problems by integrating the
needs of people, the possibilities of technology, and the requirements for program
success.</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/08.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Core Phases: Empathize
Objective: Understand your users' needs, motivations, and
challenges.
Methods: User interviews, observations, personas, and
immersion in the user environment.
Importance: Builds a foundation for designing solutions that
are rooted in real-world needs and problems.</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/09.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Core Phases: Define
Objective: Clearly articulate the user's needs and the problem
to be solved.
Methods: Synthesis of data, framing the problem statement,
theory of action.
Importance: Ensures that everyone is aligned and focused on
solving the right problem.</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/10.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Core Phases: Ideate
Objective: Generate a wide variety of potential solutions.
Methods: Brainstorming sessions, mind mapping, and lateral
thinking.
Importance: Encourages creative problem-solving and lays the
groundwork for innovative solutions.</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/11.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Core Phases: Prototype
Objective: Create low-fidelity models of the best ideas from
the ideation phase.
Methods: Sketching, mock-ups, digital wireframes.
Importance: Allows for rapid testing and iteration, helping to
identify the most viable solutions.</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/12.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Core Phases: Test
Objective: Validate the effectiveness of the prototype by
collecting user feedback.
Methods: Evaluation, user testing sessions, A/B testing,
surveys.
Importance: Provides valuable insights for refining the solution
and ensures it meets user needs before full-scale
implementation.</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/13.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Design Thinking in Educational Accountability</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/14.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Aligning Design Thinking with Educational
Accountability
Aligning Design Thinking with Educational
Understanding Users: Parents, Teachers, Students,
Administrators, and Policy Makers
Defining Problems: What issues do existing accountability
systems face? (E.g., Lack of Fairness, Inequality, Ineffective,
Obscure and Complex)
Ideation &amp; Prototyping: Development and introduction of new
indicators.</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/15.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Understanding
Aligning DesignUsers
Thinking with Educational
Objective: Identify the needs, motivations, and challenges of
all stakeholders involved in educational accountability.
Who are the Users: Parents, Teachers, Students, Policy Makers,
Educational Assessment Specialists
Methods: Stakeholder interviews, surveys, and participatory
design sessions, personas.
Importance: Builds a robust understanding of stakeholder
needs, shaping the direction of accountability system design.</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/16.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Defining Design
Aligning Problems
Thinking with Educational
Objective: Clearly state the issues and challenges that existing
accountability systems face.
Examples of Problems: Lack of fairness, inequality, inadequate
representation of student growth, etc.
Methods: Data analysis, literature reviews, and expert
consultations.
Importance: Ensures focus on solving the most pressing problems
in educational accountability, increasing the efficacy of the resulting
solutions.</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/17.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Ideation Design
Aligning &amp; Prototyping
Thinking with Educational
Objective: Develop creative and effective indicators and
dissemination strategies for educational accountability
systems.
Methods: Brainstorming sessions, prototyping workshops, and
iterative testing.
Importance: Facilitates the creation of new tools and metrics
that better capture the nuances of educational outcomes and
foster equity.</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/18.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Benefits of Applying Design Thinking to
Accountability Systems</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/19.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Transformative
Aligning Design Outcomes
Thinking with Educational
Enhanced Stakeholder Engagement: Active involvement of all
parties in the design and implementation stages.
Dynamic Indicators: Allows for the creation of more
responsive and fairer methods of assessment.
Continuous Improvement: Regular feedback loops enable
ongoing refinement of accountability systems.</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/20.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Enhanced Stakeholder
Aligning Design Engagement
Thinking with Educational
Objective: Involve all stakeholders in the process of design and
implementation, ensuring their needs and perspectives are
integrated.
Methods: Workshops, focus groups, and continuous feedback
loops.
Importance: Creates a sense of ownership among
stakeholders, leading to more successful and sustainable
solutions.</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/21.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Dynamic Indicators
Aligning Design Thinking with Educational
Objective: Develop indicators that are adaptable, fair, and
focused on defensible outcomes.
Methods: Iterative prototyping and testing, analytics, and
longitudinal studies.
Importance: Allows for indicators that can evolve with
educational paradigms, meeting the needs of a diverse student
population.</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/22.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Continuous Improvement
Aligning Design Thinking with Educational
Objective: Establish mechanisms for the ongoing refinement
and adaptation of educational accountability systems.
Methods: Regular review cycles, analytics, and user feedback
to iteratively improve the system.
Importance: Encourages a culture of continuous improvement,
ensuring the system remains effective and relevant over time.</div>
```
